verses.verse:
दृष्ट श्रुतानाम् परिशीलनेन श्रीमद् गुरुणामनुकम्पया च।
अभ्यास सद्भाव सुसंगततैश्च पुष्यन्ति विद्याः सलुसाधकानाम्।१४९।
verses.text: Through close study of what has been seen and heard, through the kindness of revered gurus, and through practice, goodwill and good company, the learning of practitioners indeed flourishes.

commentary.text: For the creation of any vidyā (learning) takes place for every living being even before birth, in the form of saṃskāra (ingrained disposition). After that, [the question is] in what order that saṃskāra is found to develop. In this context the above śloka sets out that a child with saṃskāra is by nature an imitator; whatever subjects pass along the path of his senses, he keeps taking them in as seen or heard.

When that child grows a little older, the saṃskāra shown in his actions impresses his mother and father. Then, when he is taken to an illustrious guru suited to that same saṃskāra, the guru too, seeing his saṃskāra, becomes pleased even without any service [from him], and that very pleasure, becoming a blessing, makes that saṃskāra stronger still.

Later, in adolescence, he becomes engaged in abhyāsa (practice) under the guidance of the guru. By the strength of practice, that practitioner (sādhaka) wins over the many other bad saṃskāras of the world without effort, just as a two-wheeled bicycle, moving in a set direction under the guidance of its rider, seems to have forgotten how to fall this way and that. Then the peace of mind gained from the yoga of practice in the same way gives rise to sadbhāva (goodwill). Goodwill brings that practitioner together with those who appreciate merit, in whose company he moves forward towards ever greater progress.

Sometimes, when he begins to enjoy the charming honour that has come to him without offering it to the guru, a veil of ego spreads like mist between the guru's grace and the practitioner; then it is good company that removes it.
If the grace of the Lord can have a visible form, it is good company itself.

Thus, from birth to maturity, this is the order in which learning grows strong - (1) anukaraṇa (imitation) (2) gurukṛpā (the guru's grace) (3) abhyāsa (practice) (4) sadbhāva (goodwill) (5) susaṅgati (good company) (6) ānanda (bliss)
Now, for the benefit of those imitating practitioners who do not get the shelter of a guru's grace, the following śloka is presented.
